claim: Proteotoxic stress impairs cellular homeostasis and underlies the pathogenesis of many neurodegenerative diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Proteotoxic stress impairs cellular homeostasis and underlies the pathogenesis of many neurodegenerative diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
evidence: This is a general statement about proteotoxic stress and neurodegenerative diseases that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The proteasomal and autophagic degradation of proteins are two major pathways for protein quality control in the cell.
source: The proteasomal and autophagic degradation of proteins are two major pathways for protein quality control in the cell.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific consensus about protein quality control mechanisms.

claim: A genome-wide CRISPR screen uncovered DBT as a major regulator of cytotoxicity resulting from the inhibition of the proteasome.
source: Here, we report a genome-wide CRISPR screen uncovering a major regulator of cytotoxicity resulting from the inhibition of the proteasome.
evidence: The manuscript describes conducting a genome-wide CRISPR screen and identifying DBT as a result.

claim: DBT was found to be a robust suppressor, the loss of which protects against proteasome inhibition-associated cell death through promoting clearance of ubiquitinated proteins.
source: Dihydrolipoamide branched chain transacylase E2 (DBT) was found to be a robust suppressor, the loss of which protects against proteasome inhibition-associated cell death through promoting clearance of ubiquitinated proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the CRISPR screen and subsequent validation experiments.

claim: Loss of DBT altered the metabolic and energetic status of the cell.
source: Loss of DBT altered the metabolic and energetic status of the cell and resulted in activation of autophagy in an AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent mechanism in the presence of proteasomal inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of BCAA levels and ATP/ADP ratios in DBT KO cells.

claim: Loss of DBT resulted in activation of autophagy in an AMPK-dependent mechanism in the presence of proteasomal inhibition.
source: Loss of DBT altered the metabolic and energetic status of the cell and resulted in activation of autophagy in an AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent mechanism in the presence of proteasomal inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing LC3II levels, autophagy flux measurements, and AMPK knockdown experiments.

claim: Loss of DBT protected against proteotoxicity induced by ALS-linked mutant TDP-43 in Drosophila.
source: Loss of DBT protected against proteotoxicity induced by ALS-linked mutant TDP-43 in Drosophila and mammalian neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Drosophila models showing rescue of rough eye phenotype.

claim: Loss of DBT protected against proteotoxicity induced by ALS-linked mutant TDP-43 in mammalian neurons.
source: Loss of DBT protected against proteotoxicity induced by ALS-linked mutant TDP-43 in Drosophila and mammalian neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mouse ES cell-differentiated motor neurons.

claim: DBT is upregulated in the tissues of ALS patients.
source: DBT is upregulated in the tissues of ALS patients.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and immunofluorescence analysis of spinal cord tissues from ALS patients.

claim: DBT is a master switch in the metabolic control of protein quality control with implications in neurodegenerative diseases.
source: These results demonstrate that DBT is a master switch in the metabolic control of protein quality control with implications in neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data showing DBT's role in metabolism, autophagy, and protection against proteotoxicity.

claim: Protein inclusions containing TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) are a pathological hallmark of several neurodegenerative diseases, including the majority of ALS cases and significant subsets of FTD and AD cases.
source: For instance, protein inclusions containing TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) are a pathological hallmark of several neurodegenerative diseases, including the majority of ALS cases and significant subsets of FTD and AD cases (Neumann et al., 2006; Cairns et al., 2007; Lagier-Tourenne et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The accumulation of misfolded proteins can overwhelm the protein quality control systems in the cell and lead to functional impairment or cell death.
source: The accumulation of misfolded proteins can overwhelm the protein quality control systems in the cell and lead to functional impairment or cell death (Tyedmers et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) plays a pivotal role in protein quality control.
source: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), a selective proteolytic system based on the tagging of substrate proteins with ubiquitin molecules, plays a pivotal role in protein quality control (Glickman and Ciechanover, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Autophagy mediates bulk or selective protein degradation or removal of protein aggregates in the cell.
source: Autophagy is another major pathway for protein quality control, which mediates bulk or selective protein degradation or removal of protein aggregates in the cell (Yamamoto and Yue, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Impairment of both the UPS and autophagic systems has been extensively implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Impairment of both the UPS and autophagic systems has been extensively implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases (Ciechanover and Brundin, 2003; Wong and Cuervo, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The CRISPR screen was performed on human retinal pigment epithelium (RPE1) cells through infection with single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) from the human GeCKO lentiviral pooled library.
source: The screen was performed on human retinal pigment epithelium (RPE1) cells, a genomically stable diploid cell line, through infection with single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) from the human GeCKO (Genome-Scale CRISPR Knock-out) lentiviral pooled library (Sanjana et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: MG132 is a potent and reversible proteasome inhibitor.
source: A potent and reversible proteasome inhibitor, MG132 (Kisselev and Goldberg, 2001), which is a peptide aldehyde and analog of proteasomal substrates, was applied to induce proteotoxicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 2 μM of MG132 caused lethality in most RPE1 cells within 6 days.
source: The sensitivity of RPE1 cells to proteasome inhibition was tested with MG132 treatment at a range of concentrations, with 2  μM of MG132 observed to cause lethality in most of the cells within 6 days (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The cell line that had the most potent resistance phenotype was found to harbor a specific sgRNA against the DBT gene.
source: The cell line that had the most potent resistance phenotype was found to harbor a specific sgRNA against the DBT gene.
evidence: This describes the result of the CRISPR screen.

claim: Sanger sequencing of the genomic locus targeted by the sgRNA revealed a homozygous mutation, where a 1 bp insertion in exon 2 resulted in a premature stop codon in exon 3.
source: Sanger sequencing of the genomic locus targeted by the sgRNA revealed a homozygous mutation, where a 1 bp insertion in exon 2 resulted in a premature stop codon in exon 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The loss of the C-terminal 77 amino acids from the 482 a.a. full-length protein suggests that this is a null mutant of DBT.
source: The loss of the C-terminal 77 amino acids from the 482 a.a. full-length protein suggests that this is a null mutant of DBT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequencing data and protein structure.

claim: DBT KO cells exhibited the robust phenotype of resisting MG132-induced cytotoxicity when compared to the wild-type (WT) control cells.
source: The phenotype of the DBT knockout (KO) cell line was verified through a series of cell survival experiments, in which the cells were subjected to MG132 treatment at a range of concentrations or over a period of time, and the DBT KO cells exhibited the robust phenotype of resisting MG132-induced cytotoxicity when compared to the wild-type (WT) control cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The resistance of DBT KO cells to proteasome inhibition-induced cytotoxicity was confirmed using another proteasome inhibitor, bortezomib.
source: Additionally, the resistance of DBT KO cells to proteasome inhibition-induced cytotoxicity was confirmed using another proteasome inhibitor, bortezomib. The results from the bortezomib assay were consistent with those of MG132, as the DBT KO cells consistently demonstrated better survival rates than the WT control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Knockdown of DBT in RPE1 cells by using a small hairpin RNA (shRNA) against the gene resulted in a similar phenotype of resistance to MG132-induced cell toxicity.
source: To further confirm the role of DBT in the cell survival phenotype through an independent approach of removing DBT protein, we knocked down DBT in RPE1 cells by using a small hairpin RNA (shRNA) against the gene and observed a similar phenotype, indicating that DBT deficiency indeed underlies the resistance of the cells to MG132-induced cell toxicity (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The expression of DBT' in the DBT KO cells completely restored the cell lethality phenotype induced by MG132 treatment.
source: The expression of DBT' in the DBT KO cells completely restored the cell lethality phenotype induced by MG132 treatment, as measured by the fluorescence signals from Calcein AM (Figure 1D and E), a cell-permeant dye that stains live cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: WT RPE1 cells exhibited pronounced cell death as indicated by an increase in cleaved PARP1 and Caspase 3 after treatment with 2 μM MG132 for 48 hr.
source: While WT RPE1 cells exhibited pronounced cell death as indicated by an increase in cleaved PARP1 and Caspase 3 after treatment with 2  μM MG132 for 48 hr, loss of DBT markedly suppressed the cleavage of these cell death marker proteins (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Loss of DBT markedly suppressed the cleavage of PARP1 and Caspase 3 cell death marker proteins after MG132 treatment.
source: While WT RPE1 cells exhibited pronounced cell death as indicated by an increase in cleaved PARP1 and Caspase 3 after treatment with 2  μM MG132 for 48 hr, loss of DBT markedly suppressed the cleavage of these cell death marker proteins (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Loss of DBT robustly suppresses cell toxicity induced by the proteasome inhibitor MG132.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that loss of DBT robustly suppresses cell toxicity induced by the proteasome inhibitor MG132.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: MG132 treatment led to an accumulation of poly-ubiquitinated proteins in WT cells.
source: To assess the effect of MG132-induced proteasomal inhibition on protein ubiquitination in WT and DBT KO RPE1 cells, we performed immunoblotting analysis of ubiquitinated proteins, which showed an accumulation of poly-ubiquitinated proteins in the WT cells upon the MG132 treatment, whereas the MG132-induced changes in the levels of poly-ubiquitinated proteins in the DBT KO cells were significantly reduced (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The MG132-induced changes in the levels of poly-ubiquitinated proteins in the DBT KO cells were significantly reduced compared to WT cells.
source: To assess the effect of MG132-induced proteasomal inhibition on protein ubiquitination in WT and DBT KO RPE1 cells, we performed immunoblotting analysis of ubiquitinated proteins, which showed an accumulation of poly-ubiquitinated proteins in the WT cells upon the MG132 treatment, whereas the MG132-induced changes in the levels of poly-ubiquitinated proteins in the DBT KO cells were significantly reduced (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The relative reduction in the accumulation of poly-ubiquitinated proteins in the DBT KO cells compared with those in the WT cells was observed over a period of 3 days of the MG132 treatment.
source: Moreover, the relative reduction in the accumulation of poly-ubiquitinated proteins in the DBT KO cells compared with those in the WT cells was observed over a period of 3 days of the MG132 treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), when more than half of the WT cells had died,
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was a substantial accumulation of ubiquitin-positive proteins in the WT cells upon treatment with 2 μM of MG132 for 48 hr.
source: Although the ubiquitin signal was very low without MG132 treatment, there was a substantial accumulation of ubiquitin-positive proteins in the WT cells upon treatment with 2  μM of MG132 for 48 hr. However, the MG132-induced increase in ubiquitin immunofluorescence signals was greatly diminished in the DBT KO cells when compared with the WT cells (Figure 2B), suggesting that loss of DBT suppressed the MG132-induced cell death by preventing the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The MG132-induced increase in ubiquitin immunofluorescence signals was greatly diminished in the DBT KO cells when compared with the WT cells.
source: Although the ubiquitin signal was very low without MG132 treatment, there was a substantial accumulation of ubiquitin-positive proteins in the WT cells upon treatment with 2  μM of MG132 for 48 hr. However, the MG132-induced increase in ubiquitin immunofluorescence signals was greatly diminished in the DBT KO cells when compared with the WT cells (Figure 2B), suggesting that loss of DBT suppressed the MG132-induced cell death by preventing the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Loss of DBT suppressed the MG132-induced cell death by preventing the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins.
source: Although the ubiquitin signal was very low without MG132 treatment, there was a substantial accumulation of ubiquitin-positive proteins in the WT cells upon treatment with 2  μM of MG132 for 48 hr. However, the MG132-induced increase in ubiquitin immunofluorescence signals was greatly diminished in the DBT KO cells when compared with the WT cells (Figure 2B), suggesting that loss of DBT suppressed the MG132-induced cell death by preventing the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunofluorescence data.

claim: Ubiquitin modification is a universal feature of pathological protein aggregates observed in neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Ubiquitin modification is a universal feature of pathological protein aggregates observed in neurodegenerative diseases (Alves-Rodrigues et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The MG132 treatment triggered a substantial accumulation of aggregated proteins in the WT cells.
source: The fluorescence staining indicated that the MG132 treatment triggered a substantial accumulation of aggregated proteins in the WT cells; however, the levels of the protein aggregates were significantly reduced in the DBT KO cells under the MG132 treatment (Figure 2C), consistent with the changes in the levels of poly-ubiquitinated proteins.
evidence: This is supported by ProteoStat staining data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The levels of the protein aggregates were significantly reduced in the DBT KO cells under the MG132 treatment.
source: The fluorescence staining indicated that the MG132 treatment triggered a substantial accumulation of aggregated proteins in the WT cells; however, the levels of the protein aggregates were significantly reduced in the DBT KO cells under the MG132 treatment (Figure 2C), consistent with the changes in the levels of poly-ubiquitinated proteins.
evidence: This is supported by ProteoStat staining data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Loss of DBT prevents the accumulation of protein aggregates as a result of MG132-induced proteasomal inhibition.
source: These results demonstrate that loss of DBT prevents the accumulation of protein aggregates as a result of MG132-induced proteasomal inhibition.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the protein aggregate data.

claim: The DBT KO cells had similar proteasomal activity to that of WT cells under resting states.
source: Using a luminogenic Proteasome-Glo substrate, we measured the chymotrypsin-like proteolytic activity of the proteasome in WT and DBT KO RPE1 cells. The DBT KO cells had similar proteasomal activity to that of WT cells under resting states.
evidence: This is supported by proteasome activity assay data.

claim: The MG132 treatment decreased the proteasomal activity in both WT and DBT KO cells but to the same degree.
source: Notably, the MG132 treatment decreased the proteasomal activity in both WT and DBT KO cells but to the same degree (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by proteasome activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The protein levels of proteasomal core subunits, such as PSMD1, PSMD5, and PSMD11, were unchanged between the WT and DBT KO cells before or after the MG132 treatment.
source: Furthermore, the protein levels of proteasomal core subunits, such as PSMD1, PSMD5, and PSMD11, were unchanged between the WT and DBT KO cells before or after the MG132 treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Loss of DBT does not promote proteasomal activity but prevents the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins through a proteasome-independent mechanism.
source: These results show that loss of DBT does not promote proteasomal activity but prevents the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins through a proteasome-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteasome activity and protein level data.

claim: The autophagy-lysosome pathway is an alternative mechanism for the degradation of ubiquitinated proteins.
source: The autophagy-lysosome pathway is an alternative mechanism for the degradation of ubiquitinated proteins (Kraft et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the absence of MG132 treatment, the LC3II levels were similar between WT and DBT KO cells.
source: In the absence of MG132 treatment, the LC3II levels were similar between WT and DBT KO cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data.

claim: The Bafilomycin A1-induced increase in LC3II was comparable between WT and DBT KO cells under resting conditions.
source: Treatment with the lysosome inhibitor Bafilomycin A1 blocks the degradation of LC3II, and the Bafilomycin A1-induced increase in LC3II was comparable between WT and DBT KO cells, indicating that the DBT KO cells had normal autophagy flux levels similar to those of WT cells under the resting condition (Figure 3A–C; Loos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: DBT KO cells had normal autophagy flux levels similar to those of WT cells under the resting condition.
source: Treatment with the lysosome inhibitor Bafilomycin A1 blocks the degradation of LC3II, and the Bafilomycin A1-induced increase in LC3II was comparable between WT and DBT KO cells, indicating that the DBT KO cells had normal autophagy flux levels similar to those of WT cells under the resting condition (Figure 3A–C; Loos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the LC3II data.

claim: Upon treatment with 2 μM of MG132 for 48 hr, there was a significant increase in LC3II levels in WT cells.
source: Upon the treatment with 2  μM of MG132 for 48 hr, there was a significant increase in LC3II levels in WT cells; however, the Bafilomycin A1-induced inhibition of lysosomal degradation did not further increase the LC3II levels in the WT cells, indicating that the autophagy flux was severely impaired, thereby leading to the accumulation of LC3II in these cells (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: The Bafilomycin A1-induced inhibition of lysosomal degradation did not further increase the LC3II levels in the WT cells under MG132 treatment, indicating that the autophagy flux was severely impaired.
source: Upon the treatment with 2  μM of MG132 for 48 hr, there was a significant increase in LC3II levels in WT cells; however, the Bafilomycin A1-induced inhibition of lysosomal degradation did not further increase the LC3II levels in the WT cells, indicating that the autophagy flux was severely impaired, thereby leading to the accumulation of LC3II in these cells (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the LC3II data.

claim: DBT KO cells exhibited lower levels of LC3II than the WT cells upon the MG132 treatment.
source: By contrast, the DBT KO cells exhibited lower levels of LC3II than the WT cells upon the MG132 treatment, and unlike the WT cells, these DBT KO cells showed further increase in LC3II levels after the Bafilomycin A1-induced inhibition of lysosomal degradation, indicating that the DBT KO cells had a functioning autophagy flux under the MG132-treated condition (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: DBT KO cells showed further increase in LC3II levels after the Bafilomycin A1-induced inhibition of lysosomal degradation under MG132 treatment, indicating that the DBT KO cells had a functioning autophagy flux.
source: By contrast, the DBT KO cells exhibited lower levels of LC3II than the WT cells upon the MG132 treatment, and unlike the WT cells, these DBT KO cells showed further increase in LC3II levels after the Bafilomycin A1-induced inhibition of lysosomal degradation, indicating that the DBT KO cells had a functioning autophagy flux under the MG132-treated condition (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the LC3II data.

claim: DBT KO cells showed further increase in the LC3II levels after the inhibition of lysosomal degradation with vinblastine.
source: Moreover, using another compound, vinblastine, that blocks the fusion between the autophagosome and the lysosome, we observed effects similar to those of Bafilomycin A1 that DBT KO cells showed further increase in the LC3II levels after the inhibition of lysosomal degradation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MG132-induced increases of LC3II could be observed as early as 4 hr after the treatment.
source: Time course analyses of LC3II levels indicated that MG132-induced increases of LC3II could be observed as early as 4 hr after the treatment and that DBT KO cells consistently showed higher LC3II levels than the WT control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B C).
evidence: This is supported by time course data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B C.

claim: DBT KO cells consistently showed higher LC3II levels than the WT control cells over time after MG132 treatment.
source: Time course analyses of LC3II levels indicated that MG132-induced increases of LC3II could be observed as early as 4 hr after the treatment and that DBT KO cells consistently showed higher LC3II levels than the WT control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B C).
evidence: This is supported by time course data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B C.

claim: When DBT expression was reintroduced into the DBT KO cells, the level of LC3II was decreased.
source: When DBT expression was reintroduced into the DBT KO cells, the level of LC3II was decreased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Loss of DBT enhances the function of the autophagy-lysosome pathway under the stress induced by proteasomal inhibition.
source: These results suggest that loss of DBT enhances the function of the autophagy-lysosome pathway under the stress induced by proteasomal inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the LC3II and autophagy flux data.

claim: P62 is the autophagy receptor for ubiquitinated proteins.
source: P62 is the autophagy receptor for ubiquitinated proteins (Katsuragi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the absence of MG132 treatment, the p62 levels were comparable between WT and DBT KO cells.
source: In the absence of MG132 treatment, the p62 levels were comparable between WT and DBT KO cells and were increased to similar levels upon the treatment with the lysosome inhibitor Bafilomycin A1, confirming that the DBT KO cells had normal autophagy functions under the resting condition (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: Under the MG132-induced proteotoxic condition, the WT cells showed a heightened level of p62 and there was no further increase in p62 after the Bafilomycin A1-induced inhibition of lysosomal degradation.
source: However, under the MG132-induced proteotoxic condition, the WT cells showed a heightened level of p62 and there was no further increase in p62 after the Bafilomycin A1-induced inhibition of lysosomal degradation (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: With the MG132 treatment, the DBT KO cells exhibited lower levels of p62 than the WT cells and showed a further increase in p62 after the lysosomal inhibition, confirming that the DBT KO cells had preserved the autophagic functions under the MG132-treated condition.
source: By contrast, with the MG132 treatment, the DBT KO cells exhibited lower levels of p62 than the WT cells and showed a further increase in p62 after the lysosomal inhibition, confirming that the DBT KO cells had preserved the autophagic functions under the MG132-treated condition (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: The inhibition of the autophagy-lysosome pathway with Bafilomycin A1 completely abolished the enhanced cell survival associated with loss of DBT under MG132 treatment.
source: As mentioned above, loss of DBT protected cells from MG132-induced cell death; however, the inhibition of the autophagy-lysosome pathway with Bafilomycin A1 completely abolished the enhanced cell survival associated with loss of DBT (Figure 3G), indicating that the autophagy-lysosome pathway is required for the DBT-dependent regulation of proteotoxicity under proteasomal inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The autophagy-lysosome pathway is required for the DBT-dependent regulation of proteotoxicity under proteasomal inhibition.
source: As mentioned above, loss of DBT protected cells from MG132-induced cell death; however, the inhibition of the autophagy-lysosome pathway with Bafilomycin A1 completely abolished the enhanced cell survival associated with loss of DBT (Figure 3G), indicating that the autophagy-lysosome pathway is required for the DBT-dependent regulation of proteotoxicity under proteasomal inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell viability data.

claim: DBT is a core component of the branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKD) enzyme complex, which functions in inner mitochondria to break down the essential branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), leucine, isoleucine, and valine.
source: DBT is a core component of the branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKD) enzyme complex, which functions in inner mitochondria to break down the essential branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), leucine, isoleucine, and valine (Brosnan and Brosnan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The BCKD-mediated reaction is the rate-limiting and irreversible step in the catabolism of BCAAs into acetyl-CoA or succinyl-CoA, which can be used for energy production by the citric acid cycle.
source: The BCKD-mediated reaction is the rate-limiting and irreversible step in the catabolism of BCAAs into acetyl-CoA or succinyl-CoA, which can be used for energy production by the citric acid cycle (Holeček, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The DBT KO cells exhibited significantly increased levels of BCAAs.
source: The DBT KO cells exhibited significantly increased levels of BCAAs, in line with the notion that DBT is essential for BCAA catabolism (Figure 4A, left).
evidence: This is supported by BCAA measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MG132 treatment led to a decrease in the BCAA levels in the WT cells.
source: Although MG132 treatment led to a decrease in the BCAA levels in the WT cells, the BCAA levels in the DBT KO cells remained elevated and showed no change upon the MG132 treatment (Figure 4A), confirming that the BCAA catabolism was completely blocked in the absence of DBT.
evidence: This is supported by BCAA measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The BCAA levels in the DBT KO cells remained elevated and showed no change upon the MG132 treatment, confirming that the BCAA catabolism was completely blocked in the absence of DBT.
source: Although MG132 treatment led to a decrease in the BCAA levels in the WT cells, the BCAA levels in the DBT KO cells remained elevated and showed no change upon the MG132 treatment (Figure 4A), confirming that the BCAA catabolism was completely blocked in the absence of DBT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BCAA measurement data.

claim: When the BCAA levels were increased by 6–8 folds in the culture media of WT RPE1 cells, there was no protection against MG132 toxicity.
source: When the BCAA levels were increased by 6–8 folds in the culture media of WT RPE1 cells, we did not observe any protection against MG132 toxicity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the BCAA accumulation alone was not sufficient to protect the cells from toxicity associated with the proteasomal impairment.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The BCAA accumulation alone was not sufficient to protect the cells from toxicity associated with the proteasomal impairment.
source: When the BCAA levels were increased by 6–8 folds in the culture media of WT RPE1 cells, we did not observe any protection against MG132 toxicity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the BCAA accumulation alone was not sufficient to protect the cells from toxicity associated with the proteasomal impairment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell viability data.

claim: Depletion of BCAT or BCKDHA did not affect cell survival under normal conditions.
source: Depletion of BCAT or BCKDHA did not affect cell survival under normal conditions. However, the BCAT or BCKDHA knockout cells exhibited significant resistance to MG132-induced cytotoxicity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), similar to DBT knockout cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The BCAT or BCKDHA knockout cells exhibited significant resistance to MG132-induced cytotoxicity, similar to DBT knockout cells.
source: Depletion of BCAT or BCKDHA did not affect cell survival under normal conditions. However, the BCAT or BCKDHA knockout cells exhibited significant resistance to MG132-induced cytotoxicity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), similar to DBT knockout cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: It is not the accumulation of BCAAs but the blockade of the BCAA catabolism that leads to resistance to MG132-induced toxicity.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that it is not the accumulation of BCAAs but the blockade of the BCAA catabolism that leads to resistance to MG132-induced toxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BCAA and cell viability data.

claim: Under normal conditions, the DBT KO cells showed ATP/ADP ratios comparable to those of WT cells.
source: Under normal conditions, the DBT KO cells showed ATP/ADP ratios comparable to those of WT cells.
evidence: This is supported by ATP/ADP ratio measurement data.

claim: The MG132 treatment slightly decreased the ATP/ADP ratios in the WT cells.
source: The MG132 treatment slightly decreased the ATP/ADP ratios in the WT cells; however, the MG132-treated DBT KO cells exhibited significantly decreased ATP/ADP ratios compared to the untreated DBT KO cells or the WT cells with or without the MG132 treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by ATP/ADP ratio measurement data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The MG132-treated DBT KO cells exhibited significantly decreased ATP/ADP ratios compared to the untreated DBT KO cells or the WT cells with or without the MG132 treatment.
source: The MG132 treatment slightly decreased the ATP/ADP ratios in the WT cells; however, the MG132-treated DBT KO cells exhibited significantly decreased ATP/ADP ratios compared to the untreated DBT KO cells or the WT cells with or without the MG132 treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by ATP/ADP ratio measurement data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When WT cells were examined, increasing the glucose concentrations in the media from 17.5 mM to 70 mM or 140 mM did not affect the sensitivity of the WT cells to MG132 toxicity.
source: When WT cells were examined, increasing the glucose concentrations in the media from 17.5 mM to 70 mM or 140 mM did not affect the sensitivity of the WT cells to MG132 toxicity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The increased glucose levels significantly decreased the survival of DBT KO cells under MG132 treatment in a glucose-concentration-dependent manner.
source: In contrast, when the cell survival of DBT KO cells was examined, the increased glucose levels significantly decreased the survival of DBT KO cells under MG132 treatment in a glucose-concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), in accordance with the notion that reduction in ATP levels contributed to the resistance of DBT KO cells to MG132 toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Glucose starvation rendered WT cells more resistant to MG132-induced toxicity.
source: Furthermore, glucose starvation rendered WT cells more resistant to MG132-induced toxicity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), consistent with the notion that reduction in ATP levels contributed to the cellular resistance to the toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Loss of DBT combined with proteasomal inhibition led to a significant decrease in the ATP/ADP ratios, which correlated with the preservation of autophagic activities and the resistance to cell death induced by the proteasomal inhibition.
source: Together, these results indicate that loss of DBT combined with proteasomal inhibition led to a significant decrease in the ATP/ADP ratios, which correlated with the preservation of autophagic activities and the resistance to cell death induced by the proteasomal inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ATP/ADP ratio and cell viability data.

claim: AMPK is a highly conserved sensor of cellular energy changes and is activated by increasing levels of AMP or ADP coupled with falling ATP.
source: AMPK is a highly conserved sensor of cellular energy changes and is activated by increasing levels of AMP or ADP coupled with falling ATP (Mihaylova and Shaw, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The levels of phosphorylated AMPK-T172 were not significantly changed in the DBT KO cells under the resting condition.
source: The levels of phosphorylated AMPK-T172 were not significantly changed in the DBT KO cells under the resting condition; however, upon the MG132 treatment, the DBT KO cells exhibited significantly higher levels of phosphorylated AMPK-T172 than the WT cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Upon the MG132 treatment, the DBT KO cells exhibited significantly higher levels of phosphorylated AMPK-T172 than the WT cells.
source: The levels of phosphorylated AMPK-T172 were not significantly changed in the DBT KO cells under the resting condition; however, upon the MG132 treatment, the DBT KO cells exhibited significantly higher levels of phosphorylated AMPK-T172 than the WT cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The total level of AMPK was not changed by loss of DBT or the MG132 treatment alone.
source: The total level of AMPK was not changed by loss of DBT or the MG132 treatment alone (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: AMPK was activated in cells under the MG132-induced proteotoxic stress in the absence of DBT.
source: These data indicated that AMPK was activated in cells under the MG132-induced proteotoxic stress in the absence of DBT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phosphorylated AMPK data.

claim: The AMPK knockdown abolished the resistance of the DBT KO cells to the MG132-induced cytotoxicity.
source: The AMPK knockdown abolished the resistance of the DBT KO cells to the MG132-induced cytotoxicity. Under the MG132-treated conditions, the AMPK knockdown did not affect the survival of WT RPE1 cells; however, it significantly decreased the survival of DBT KO cells to a level comparable to that of WT cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Under the MG132-treated conditions, the AMPK knockdown did not affect the survival of WT RPE1 cells.
source: The AMPK knockdown abolished the resistance of the DBT KO cells to the MG132-induced cytotoxicity. Under the MG132-treated conditions, the AMPK knockdown did not affect the survival of WT RPE1 cells; however, it significantly decreased the survival of DBT KO cells to a level comparable to that of WT cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The AMPK inhibitor Compound C abolished the protective effects of loss of DBT and rendered the DBT KO cells sensitive to the MG132 treatment.
source: To confirm the role of the AMPK signaling in the cell survival phenotype of DBT KO cells, we applied an AMPK inhibitor, Compound C (Zhou et al., 2001), and found that it also abolished the protective effects of loss of DBT and rendered the DBT KO cells sensitive to the MG132 treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The AMPK agonist EX229 promoted the resistance to MG132-induced toxicity in both WT and DBT KO cells.
source: Conversely, using an AMPK agonist EX229, also known as compound 991 (Xiao et al., 2013; Lai et al., 2014), we found that the AMPK agonist promoted the resistance to MG132-induced toxicity in both WT and DBT KO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: AMPK is a key player in the resistance of DBT KO cells against MG132-induced toxicity.
source: These results indicate that AMPK is a key player in the resistance of DBT KO cells against MG132-induced toxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the AMPK knockdown and inhibitor data.

claim: AMPK is a principal regulator of autophagy.
source: Since AMPK is a principal regulator of autophagy, we tested the role of AMPK in the autophagy activation in the DBT KO cells under MG132-induced proteotoxic stress.
evidence: This reflects established scientific knowledge about AMPK's role.

claim: The knockdown of AMPK via shRNAs significantly reduced the LC3 protein levels.
source: The knockdown of AMPK via shRNAs significantly reduced the LC3 protein levels, and quantification of LC3II levels before and after Bafilomycin A1-medicated inhibition of lysosomal degradation indicated that the autophagy flux was significantly reduced by the downregulation of AMPK (Figure 5A), consistent with the increased vulnerability of the DBT KO cells to the MG132-induced proteotoxic stress (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The autophagy flux was significantly reduced by the downregulation of AMPK.
source: The knockdown of AMPK via shRNAs significantly reduced the LC3 protein levels, and quantification of LC3II levels before and after Bafilomycin A1-medicated inhibition of lysosomal degradation indicated that the autophagy flux was significantly reduced by the downregulation of AMPK (Figure 5A), consistent with the increased vulnerability of the DBT KO cells to the MG132-induced proteotoxic stress (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the LC3II data.

claim: The activation of AMPK promotes autophagy through several downstream effectors, including serine/threonine-protein kinase ULK1 and mTOR signaling.
source: The activation of AMPK promotes autophagy through several downstream effectors, including serine/threonine-protein kinase ULK1 and mTOR signaling (Mihaylova and Shaw, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: ULK1 is an important regulator of autophagosome biogenesis and can be activated by AMPK signaling.
source: ULK1 is an important regulator of autophagosome biogenesis and can be activated by AMPK signaling (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the absence of MG132 treatment, there was no difference in the levels of total ULK1 protein or its activity, as measured by the phosphorylation at its serine 371 (S371) site.
source: In the absence of MG132 treatment, there was no difference in the levels of total ULK1 protein or its activity, as measured by the phosphorylation at its serine 371 (S371) site (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Upon the treatment with 2 μM of MG132 for 48 hr, the DBT KO cells exhibited a significant increase in the phosphorylation of ULK1-S371.
source: Upon the treatment with 2 μM of MG132 for 48 hr, there was little change in the ULK1 activity in WT RPE1 cells; however, the DBT KO cells exhibited a significant increase in the phosphorylation of ULK1-S371 (Figure 5B), indicating that loss of DBT specifically induced the activation of ULK1 under the MG132 treatment, concomitant with the AMPK activation under this condition (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Loss of DBT specifically induced the activation of ULK1 under the MG132 treatment, concomitant with the AMPK activation under this condition.
source: Upon the treatment with 2 μM of MG132 for 48 hr, there was little change in the ULK1 activity in WT RPE1 cells; however, the DBT KO cells exhibited a significant increase in the phosphorylation of ULK1-S371 (Figure 5B), indicating that loss of DBT specifically induced the activation of ULK1 under the MG132 treatment, concomitant with the AMPK activation under this condition (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the ULK1 phosphorylation data.

claim: The elevated expression of DBT significantly decreased the levels of phosphorylated ULK1 and phosphorylated AMPK in both WT and DBT KO cells.
source: Conversely, the elevated expression of DBT significantly decreased the levels of phosphorylated ULK1 and phosphorylated AMPK in both WT and DBT KO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Loss of DBT specifically induces the activation of the AMPK-ULK1 signaling under MG132 treatment.
source: These results indicate that loss of DBT specifically induces the activation of the AMPK-ULK1 signaling under MG132 treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the AMPK and ULK1 phosphorylation data.

claim: AMPK regulates the mTOR signaling by phosphorylating TSC2 on serine 1387 (S1387).
source: AMPK is reported to regulate the mTOR signaling by phosphorylating TSC2 on serine 1387 (S1387) (Mihaylova and Shaw, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Phosphorylation of TSC2-S1387 enhances the activity of TSC2 as a Rheb GAP, leading to the inhibition of mTOR.
source: Phosphorylation of TSC2-S1387 enhances the activity of TSC2 as a Rheb GAP, leading to the inhibition of mTOR.
evidence: This reflects established scientific knowledge about TSC2 function.

claim: There was little difference in the phosphorylation levels of TSC2 between the WT and DBT KO cells in the absence of MG132 treatment.
source: There was little difference in the phosphorylation levels of TSC2 between the WT and DBT KO cells in the absence of MG132 treatment; however, under the treatment of 2 μM of MG132 for 48 hr, the DBT KO cells exhibited significantly higher levels of phosphorylated TSC2-S1387, while the WT cells did not show any change in the phosphorylation levels of TSC2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Under the treatment of 2 μM of MG132 for 48 hr, the DBT KO cells exhibited significantly higher levels of phosphorylated TSC2-S1387, while the WT cells did not show any change in the phosphorylation levels of TSC2.
source: There was little difference in the phosphorylation levels of TSC2 between the WT and DBT KO cells in the absence of MG132 treatment; however, under the treatment of 2 μM of MG132 for 48 hr, the DBT KO cells exhibited significantly higher levels of phosphorylated TSC2-S1387, while the WT cells did not show any change in the phosphorylation levels of TSC2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The AMPK-TSC2-mTOR signaling is another mechanism through which loss of DBT leads to autophagic activation under proteasomal impairment.
source: These results suggest that the AMPK-TSC2-mTOR signaling is another mechanism through which loss of DBT leads to autophagic activation under proteasomal impairment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TSC2 phosphorylation data.

claim: The increase in the mTOR activity as a result of TSC1 knockdown led to a significant reduction in LC3II protein levels as well as in the autophagy flux.
source: The increase in the mTOR activity as a result of TSC1 knockdown, as confirmed by the upregulated S6K phosphorylation (Figure 5C), led to a significant reduction in LC3II protein levels as well as in the autophagy flux measured by the LC3II ratios before and after Bafilomycin treatment, confirming that the autophagic activation in the DBT KO cells was dependent on the inhibition of mTOR signaling (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The autophagic activation in the DBT KO cells was dependent on the inhibition of mTOR signaling.
source: The increase in the mTOR activity as a result of TSC1 knockdown, as confirmed by the upregulated S6K phosphorylation (Figure 5C), led to a significant reduction in LC3II protein levels as well as in the autophagy flux measured by the LC3II ratios before and after Bafilomycin treatment, confirming that the autophagic activation in the DBT KO cells was dependent on the inhibition of mTOR signaling (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the LC3II and autophagy flux data.

claim: The knockdown of TSC1 abolished the enhanced survival phenotype of the DBT KO cells under the MG132 treatment.
source: Furthermore, in accordance with the changes in autophagic activities, the knockdown of TSC1 abolished the enhanced survival phenotype of the DBT KO cells under the MG132 treatment (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The mTOR agonist MHY1485 abolished the protective effects of loss of DBT and rendered the DBT KO cells sensitive to the MG132 treatment.
source: To confirm the role of the mTOR signaling in the cell survival phenotype of DBT KO cells, we applied an mTOR agonist, MHY1485 (Choi et al., 2012), and found that it also abolished the protective effects of loss of DBT and rendered the DBT KO cells sensitive to the MG132 treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Treatment with an mTOR inhibitor, RAD001 or AZD8055, increased the resistance of WT cells to MG132-induced toxicity.
source: Conversely, treatment with an mTOR inhibitor, RAD001 or AZD8055 (Beuvink et al., 2005; Willems et al., 2012), increased the resistance of WT cells to MG132-induced toxicity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The mTOR signaling plays a key role in the resistance of DBT KO cells to the proteasomal inhibition-induced toxicity.
source: These results demonstrate that the mTOR signaling plays a key role in the resistance of DBT KO cells to the proteasomal inhibition-induced toxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TSC1 knockdown and mTOR modulator data.

claim: Neurodegeneration-associated protein misfolding and aggregation often lead to impairment of the proteasome.
source: Neurodegeneration-associated protein misfolding and aggregation often lead to impairment of the proteasome (Ciechanover and Brundin, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: ALS-linked mutant TDP-43 proteins, including the M337V variant, are prone to misfolding and aggregation.
source: ALS-linked mutant TDP-43 proteins, including the M337V variant, are prone to misfolding and aggregation, providing a disease-related molecular model for studying proteotoxicity (Johnson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The WT cells expressing TDP-43M337 showed significantly lower cell viability than those expressing the control protein.
source: The WT cells expressing TDP-43M337 showed significantly lower cell viability than those expressing the control protein, indicating that the WT cells were highly sensitive to TDP-43M337-induced proteotoxicity (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The DBT KO cells exhibited significantly higher levels of cell survival than the WT cells when expressing TDP-43M337.
source: However, the DBT KO cells exhibited significantly higher levels of cell survival than the WT cells when expressing TDP-43M337, indicating strong protection by the loss of DBT.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data.

claim: Motor neurons differentiated from mouse embryonic stem cells showed marked sensitivity to virally expressed TDP-43M337 when compared to the control GFP protein.
source: We employed motor neurons differentiated from mouse embryonic stem cells (Zhang et al., 2020), which showed marked sensitivity to virally expressed TDP-43M337 when compared to the control GFP protein, as shown by the significant neuronal loss with the TDP-43M337 expression (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by neuronal viability data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The knockdown of DBT by specific shRNAs significantly rescued the neuronal loss with the TDP-43M337 expression.
source: Importantly, the knockdown of DBT by specific shRNAs significantly rescued the neuronal loss with the TDP-43M337 expression, as compared to the non-targeting control shRNAs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by neuronal viability data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Loss of DBT resulted in robust protection against TDP-43-associated proteotoxicity.
source: These results demonstrate that loss of DBT resulted in robust protection against TDP-43-associated proteotoxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell and neuronal viability data.

claim: TDP-43M337V transiently expressed in the DBT KO RPE1 cells showed substantially lower protein levels than that expressed in the WT cells.
source: In immunoblotting analysis, TDP-43M337V transiently expressed in the DBT KO RPE1 cells showed substantially lower protein levels than that expressed in the WT cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The degradation of TDP-43M337V took place at a much faster rate in the DBT KO cells than in the WT cells.
source: As analyzed by immunoblotting of TDP-43M337V over a period of time after cycloheximide-induced inhibition of protein synthesis, the degradation of TDP-43M337V took place at a much faster rate in the DBT KO cells than in the WT cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The half-life of TDP-43M337V was estimated to be over 24 hr in the WT cells but only ~4.5 hr in the DBT KO cells.
source: The half-life of TDP-43M337V was estimated to be over 24 hr in the WT cells but only ~4.5 hr in the DBT KO cells.
evidence: This is based on the cycloheximide chase assay data.

claim: The DBT KO cells exhibited a higher degree of autophagy flux than the WT cells when expressing TDP-43M337V.
source: Furthermore, consistent with the faster turnover rate of TDP-43M337V, the DBT KO cells exhibited a higher degree of autophagy flux than the WT cells, as measured by LC3II levels before and after the Bafilomycin treatment (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The elevated expression of TDP-43M337V selectively increased the levels of phosphorylated AMPK in the DBT KO cells but not in the WT cells.
source: Additionally, the elevated expression of TDP-43M337V selectively increased the levels of phosphorylated AMPK in the DBT KO cells but not in the WT cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of DBT promoted the clearance of TDP-43M337V and reduced its proteotoxicity through enhanced AMPK signaling and autophagic functions.
source: These data indicate that loss of DBT promoted the clearance of TDP-43M337V and reduced its proteotoxicity through enhanced AMPK signaling and autophagic functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TDP-43 turnover, autophagy flux, and AMPK data.

claim: The knockdown of the DBT homolog produced a significant rescue of the TDP-43M337V-induced rough eye phenotype in Drosophila, resulting in a smoother eye appearance and increased pigmentation.
source: By crossing with a transgenic strain with stable RNAi-induced reduction of the Drosophila homolog of human DBT, CG5599 (St Pierre et al., 2014), we found that the knockdown of the DBT homolog produced a significant rescue of the TDP-43M337V-induced rough eye phenotype, resulting in a smoother eye appearance and increased pigmentation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by Drosophila eye phenotype data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: When DBT KO flies were crossed with TDP-43M337V transgenic flies, a similar protection against the rough eye phenotype was observed.
source: When we crossed the DBT KO flies with TDP-43M337V transgenic flies, a similar protection against the rough eye phenotype was observed (Figure 6F), indicating that loss of DBT protects against TDP-43-associated neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is supported by Drosophila eye phenotype data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Loss of DBT protects against TDP-43-associated neurodegeneration.
source: When we crossed the DBT KO flies with TDP-43M337V transgenic flies, a similar protection against the rough eye phenotype was observed (Figure 6F), indicating that loss of DBT protects against TDP-43-associated neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Drosophila eye phenotype data.

claim: WT RPE1 cells expressing polyQ showed significantly lower cell viability than DBT KO cells.
source: In cell survival assays, we found that WT RPE1 cells expressing polyQ showed significantly lower cell viability than DBT KO cells, indicating that loss of DBT protects against polyQ-induced proteotoxicity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Loss of DBT protects against polyQ-induced proteotoxicity.
source: In cell survival assays, we found that WT RPE1 cells expressing polyQ showed significantly lower cell viability than DBT KO cells, indicating that loss of DBT protects against polyQ-induced proteotoxicity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell viability data.

claim: PolyQ transiently expressed in the DBT KO cells exhibited substantially lower protein levels than those in WT cells.
source: In immunoblotting analysis, we found that polyQ transiently expressed in the DBT KO cells exhibited substantially lower protein levels than those in WT cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that the resistance of the DBT KO cells to polyQ-induced proteotoxicity was associated with enhanced turnover of the polyQ protein.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The resistance of the DBT KO cells to polyQ-induced proteotoxicity was associated with enhanced turnover of the polyQ protein.
source: In immunoblotting analysis, we found that polyQ transiently expressed in the DBT KO cells exhibited substantially lower protein levels than those in WT cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that the resistance of the DBT KO cells to polyQ-induced proteotoxicity was associated with enhanced turnover of the polyQ protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunoblot data.

claim: Significant protection against eye degeneration was observed in both DBT RNAi and KO flies in the polyQ transgenic fly model.
source: Based on the analysis of the rough eye phenotype in the polyQ transgenic fly model, we observed significant protection against eye degeneration in both DBT RNAi and KO flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by Drosophila eye phenotype data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: The evolutionarily conserved regulatory effects of DBT on proteotoxicity are likely broad-spectrum.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the evolutionarily conserved regulatory effects of DBT on proteotoxicity are likely broad-spectrum.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TDP-43 and polyQ data across different model systems.

claim: DBT protein levels were significantly elevated in the majority of ALS cases compared to non-neurological controls.
source: Although the immunoblot signals showed variability among the individuals, we found that DBT protein levels were significantly elevated in the majority of ALS cases (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the control cases, DBT could be seen clearly expressed in motor neurons.
source: In the control cases, DBT could be seen clearly expressed in motor neurons, which are characterized by their large soma and unique nuclear morphologies (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Compared with the controls, the DBT immunofluorescence signals showed much higher intensity and broader distribution across the spinal cord sections in ALS cases.
source: Compared with the controls, the DBT immunofluorescence signals showed much higher intensity and broader distribution across the spinal cord sections, suggesting elevated levels of DBT in neuronal soma and neurites (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Stronger signals of DBT immunofluorescence could be detected in large neuronal cell bodies in the ALS cases.
source: Indeed, stronger signals of DBT immunofluorescence could be detected in large neuronal cell bodies in the ALS cases (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The DBT-mediated regulation of protein quality control is compromised in the disease-relevant tissues of ALS patients.
source: These observations suggest that the DBT-mediated regulation of protein quality control is compromised in the disease-relevant tissues of ALS patients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the elevated DBT levels in ALS patient tissues.

claim: DBT is a master switch in the metabolic control of protein quality control.
source: The present study uncovers a major regulator of protein quality control through an unbiased genetic screen and demonstrates the signaling pathway through which DBT regulates autophagic activation under stress induced by proteasomal inhibition (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claim: The observations of DBT's robust regulatory effects on the proteotoxicity in models of neurodegenerative diseases and the upregulation of DBT in ALS patient tissues suggest that DBT is an important player in the pathogenesis of the disease.
source: The observations of DBT's robust regulatory effects on the proteotoxicity in models of neurodegenerative diseases and the upregulation of DBT in ALS patient tissues suggest that DBT is an important player in the pathogenesis of the disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined experimental and patient data.

claim: Recent studies in C. elegans suggested that BCAA metabolism plays complicated roles in the regulation of the ubiquitin-proteasome system, with deficiency in components of the BCKD complex negatively impacting the ubiquitin-proteasome activity.
source: Recent studies in C. elegans suggested that BCAA metabolism plays complicated roles in the regulation of the ubiquitin-proteasome system, with deficiency in components of the BCKD complex negatively impacting the ubiquitin-proteasome activity (Ravanelli et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Elevated levels of BCAAs are associated with inhibition of autophagy due to their ability to activate mTORC1.
source: Conventionally, elevated levels of BCAAs are associated with inhibition of autophagy due to their ability to activate mTORC1 (Zhenyukh et al., 2017), the nutrient sensor that negatively regulates autophagy (Dunlop and Tee, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ATP-producing OXPHOS complexes are sensitive to the regulation of protein quality control, as its many components are regulated by proteasomal degradation.
source: The ATP-producing OXPHOS complexes are sensitive to the regulation of protein quality control, as its many components are regulated by proteasomal degradation (Szczepanowska and Trifunovic, 2021), consistent with our observation of lower ATP levels upon treatment with the proteasome inhibitor.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: DBT-dependent BCAA catabolism is a critical source of energy production under the condition of proteasomal inhibition.
source: We also found that the DBT deficiency decreased the intracellular ATP levels under the condition of proteasomal inhibition, suggesting that DBT-dependent BCAA catabolism is a critical source of energy production under the condition of proteasomal inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATP/ADP ratio data.

claim: The net outcome of better preservation of autophagic activities, upon inhibition of both proteasomal degradation and BCAA catabolism, underlies the important roles of the energy metabolism and the cognate AMPK signaling as the driving force for the autophagic activation under these conditions.
source: Furthermore, the net outcome of better preservation of autophagic activities, upon inhibition of both proteasomal degradation and BCAA catabolism, underlies the important roles of the energy metabolism and the cognate AMPK signaling, which regulates autophagy regulators including mTOR and ULK1 (Alers et al., 2012), as the driving force for the autophagic activation under these conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined metabolic, AMPK, and autophagy data.

claim: Defective BCAA catabolism is associated with metabolic disorders, such as maple syrup urine disease, insulin resistance, and diabetes.
source: Defective BCAA catabolism is associated with metabolic disorders, such as maple syrup urine disease, insulin resistance, and diabetes (Yoon, 2016; Holeček, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Abnormal regulation of the levels and metabolism of BCAAs has been implicated in a variety of other human pathological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, cancer, and liver diseases.
source: Abnormal regulation of the levels and metabolism of BCAAs has been implicated in a variety of other human pathological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, cancer, and liver diseases (Dimou et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.
